provenance: T-R44, from PR #32 CI run 32626835735. ADR-019's Ruling has said "one per (suite, environment)" since it was written; `published-band-matches-the-ledger` had no such dimension and read every `history.jsonl` row the process could see. On CI that is a strictly larger set than the committed ledger: `.github/workflows/eval.yml` runs `--suite invariant` first, that run appends its own row on slower hardware to the job's copy of the file, and `--suite fast` then grades ADR-019 §3's locally-measured band against a ledger whose slowest row at that count is CI's. Red on CI, green locally, on the same tree. `main` passes only by coincidence — at the shipped case count CI's number and this laptop's happen to derive the same ceiling — and it had already cost something: M35 moved a new invariant case into `fast` to keep §3's band on the count `main` measured. Every history row now carries an `env` tag (`evals/run.py` `env_tag()`: `EVAL_ENV` if set, else `ci` when the runner sets `CI`, else `local`) and ADR-019 §6 item 9 (environment) filters the ledger to the band's own environment before any other item reads a row. The tag is deliberately NOT derived from the effective `EVAL_WALL_BUDGET_S_*`, which is the obvious candidate and is wrong in exactly the case that produced the defect: CI's `invariant` ceiling is 20 and so is this laptop's, so both environments would have shared a tag on the very suite that broke. This case is driven with a synthetic ledger because the defect cannot be reproduced from the committed one — no CI run's wall clock ever reaches it, which is the other half of the same root cause (T-R51, closed in ADR-019 §5/§7 by labelling CI's four numbers as hand-read values of eval-gate run 32561162459 attempts 1-4 rather than by making CI commit a row). Five things are asserted, not one: the foreign row is excluded; the SAME row measured here still reddens the band, so the filter is a filter and not a hole; an untagged row is read as `local`, which is what every row written before T-R44 is; a band naming an environment the ledger holds no rows for hits the `no_recorded_run_at` precondition instead of passing for want of anything to compare against; and two suites banded in different environments in one call do not share a filtered ledger — that last one is here because the first draft of the filter rebound `_band_wrong`'s `rows` parameter, which is invisible for as long as every published band names the same environment, and this repo publishes exactly one.

triage.note: tagged invariant and fast, like its two siblings, because the band subsystem is graded on every gate run. It costs nothing beyond `_band_wrong` on four synthetic two-row ledgers — no ledger read, no network, no spend. What it does NOT reach: this repo publishes exactly one environment's bands (`local`), so item 9 (environment) has one environment to grade here and the `ci` half of `env_tag()` is exercised by nothing but `CI=1` on a laptop (T-R74).
triage.watched_red: Four ways, three of them against code that shipped. (1) The live defect, against the REAL committed ledger and the real check, before anything was changed: a CI-shaped `invariant` row (17.5s, 53 cases, `dirty: false`) appended to `evals/report/history.jsonl` made `published-band-matches-the-ledger` report [{suite: invariant, published_slowest: 13.32, derives_ceiling: 20, ledger_slowest: 17.5, ledger_derives: 25, runs: 103}, {suite: invariant, ceiling: 20, required_by_adr013_rule: 25, ledger_slowest: 17.5}] — the band ADR-019 §3 measured on this laptop, reddened by a run from another machine. That is T-R44 in one command. (2) This case itself, written first and run against the env-blind `_band_wrong` that shipped: [{foreign_row_reddened_the_band: [{suite: s, published_slowest: 12.92, derives_ceiling: 15, ledger_slowest: 16.02, ledger_derives: 20, runs: 2}, {suite: s, ceiling: 15.0, required_by_adr013_rule: 20, ledger_slowest: 16.02}]}, {band_for_an_unrecorded_environment_stayed_green: [ ... the same two entries ... ]}] — the numbers are PR #32's own (12.92s local band, 16.02s CI row). Assertions 2 and 3 were green there and mean nothing on their own: with no filter at all, a slower row of any label reddens the band. (3) The filter deleted again after the fix, which is the mutation that holds assertions 1 and 4 up: the same two keys, now carrying the environment they were judged in — {foreign_row_reddened_the_band: [{suite: s, env: local, ...}]} and {band_for_an_unrecorded_environment_stayed_green: [{suite: s, env: ci, ...}]}. (4) `_LEGACY_ENV` set to `unknown`, which is assertion 3's mutation: {untagged_legacy_row_was_not_read_as_local: []} — the untagged row silently left the band's evidence. Worth recording that `published-band-matches-the-ledger` stayed GREEN under that same mutation, which falsified the first draft of ADR-019 §7: the bands in §2 and §3 cite rows recorded after the tag existed, so nothing in the live ledger holds the legacy reading up and the §7 sentence claiming otherwise was rewritten to say so. (5) The rebind restored — `rows = env_rows = [...]`, which is what the filter was when it was first written: {one_environments_filter_leaked_into_the_next: [{suite: b, env: ci, no_recorded_run_at: 1}]}, the second suite judged against the first's already-filtered ledger. Nothing else in the tree sees it, because both bands published here are `local`. Item 9 (environment) was watched red from the other side too, in the sibling check: the `invariant` band sentence relabelled `ci` gives {suite: invariant, env: ci, no_recorded_run_at: 54}, and item 9 deleted from §6's list with its references left standing gives four `reference_does_not_name_its_item` entries at once — in the ADR twice, in README, and in this file's own comment.
